item.title: A train was delayed by a solar storm. But something didn't add up.
item.description:
Waypoint is curating and commenting on third-party reporting. Original publisher: ScienceDaily.
Summary: Scientists have cracked a 178-year-old mystery surrounding a train delayed by a solar storm, revealing that the famous incident happened in 1848 rather than 1841. The discovery rewrites the early history of space weather and highlights a threat that still endangers modern power grids, satellites, and communication systems.

item.title: NASA spots a giant patch of Moon-like rock on Earth
item.description:
Waypoint is curating and commenting on third-party reporting. Original publisher: ScienceDaily.
Summary: An astronaut aboard the International Space Station photographed a remarkable formation in Madagascar that looks surprisingly similar to the Moon’s bright highlands. Made of anorthosite, a rock abundant on the lunar surface, the formation dates back at least 600 million years and bears the scars of ancient continental collisions.

item.title: Salt marshes are proving to be powerful allies in building a climate-resilient coastline
item.description:
Waypoint is curating and commenting on third-party reporting. Original publisher: Phys.org.
Summary: Salt marsh sediment and vegetation can remain largely intact even during extreme storm surges. This was demonstrated in a large-scale experiment in which researchers transported sections of salt marsh to an experimental facility capable of producing the world's largest artificial waves. The results show how salt marshes can contribute to natural coastal protection, both in the Netherlands and beyond.

item.title: How life on Earth experiences climate change
item.description:
Waypoint is curating and commenting on third-party reporting. Original publisher: Phys.org.
Summary: Climate change can look very different at the scale of a forest, field or hillside. A new review shows how changes in vegetation and atmospheric conditions can cause local microclimates to warm at very different rates from the regional climate—and why this matters for understanding how biodiversity will respond to climate change.
Waypoint’s Take: An outdoor reader can treat this as field context — read plant communities as living context, not background decoration. Keep the publisher’s claims provisional until you read the original. Dashboard conditions can sit beside this report before you leave.
